item.description:
Authors: Ellen McCreedy, Ann Reddy, Laura Dionne, Grace F Wittenberg, Nichole E. Stetten, Nate Hunkins, Martha Etzell, Aimee van Denberghe et al.

Source: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution

Abstract: Summary Key points Hospital admissions increase the risk of delirium, falls, and accelerated cognitive and physical decline in older adults. Providing real‐time clinical and discharge support information to emergency room providers may reduce unnecessary hospitalizations. This pilot study demonstrated that electronic admission, discharge, and transfer notifications can be used to alert accountable care organization providers when patients enter the emergency room to provide timely care management. Why does this paper matter? This is the first pilot study to use electronic admission, discharge, and transfer notifications, coupled with a structured care management response, to reduce unnecessary hospitalizations in a community‐based accountable care organization. Case managers self‐reported a hospital diversion rate of 11%; a formal efficacy study is needed to validate these results.

item.title: Decoding Modern Health Myths: Gene-Environment Interactions, the Psychology of Addiction, and the Reality of Endocrine Physiology
item.description:
Authors: Muhammad (Sam) Salman

Source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution

Abstract: This report examines the prevalence of health reductionism across respiratory pathology, behavioral psychology, and endocrinology. It argues that complex physiological outcomes are often incorrectly attributed to single environmental factors or systemic hormone levels, ignoring vital gene-environment interactions. By analyzing the genetic underpinnings of smoking-related diseases and the localized mechanical nature of muscle hypertrophy, the report dismantles common public health myths. Furthermore, it addresses the psychological barriers to addiction recovery and the medical risks associated with unregulated hormone therapies. Ultimately, a multidisciplinary approach is required to foster a scientifically rigorous understanding of human health.

item.title: When Resilience Becomes Risk: How Cybersecurity Incidents Reshape Supply Chain Recovery Strategies
item.description:
Authors: Xuecong Lu, Junyi Yang, Chunming Shi, Jie Mi, Si Liu

Source: Journal of the Association for Information Systems

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution

Abstract: Digital supply chains rely on tightly integrated information systems that improve coordination and resilience but also increase cybersecurity vulnerability. This study examines how cybersecurity incidents affect operational recovery performance and how these effects depend on firms’ pre-incident recovery structure and cybersecurity governance. We define Cyber-Structural Misalignment as a condition in which digital connectivity exceeds governance capacity to manage cyber risk. We argue that cyber incidents weaken operational recovery, that redundancy and digital integration can amplify this effect, and that strong cybersecurity governance mitigates disruption and supports recovery.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an omnipresent support technology for a variety of decisions. Abstract: Phishing remains a major cybersecurity threat, yet existing training often fails to drive behavioral change. This study examines employees’ experiences with current cybersecurity training and their attitudes toward AI-based solutions. Drawing on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and Protection Motivation Theory (PMT), we design a survey to investigate these factors. Using data from 192 employees, results show that while current training is informative, it lacks engagement and effectiveness. Employees express a strong interest in AI-based training; however, adoption is constrained by privacy concerns and limited organizational support, highlighting key tensions between perceived benefits and risks.

Authors: Benedict Lewis Abotsi

Source: Journal of the Association for Information Systems

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution

Abstract: Psychological ownership of IT (POIT) has been studied as a static antecedent. This paper proposes that POIT evolves across three stages: initial adoption, continued use, and habitual use. We develop a longitudinal model where POIT transitions from an antecedent of use to a consequence of routinized use. We provide falsifiable criteria for testing causal inversion, specify boundary conditions, and identify cognitive offloading as the underlying mechanism.
